# Terminal mux internals → Duo overhaul

A learning-and-prototyping project on terminal multiplexer internals, feeding
the Duo redesign. Each numbered handoff is self-contained: open one Claude Code
chat per handoff, paste or reference the file, and work it to its deliverable.

## How to use this project

1. Put your copies of `multi-backend-feasibility.md` and
   `procrastivity-cli-architecture.md` into `inputs/`. Handoff 09 consumes them.
2. Work handoffs in roughly this order (see the dependency graph below).
3. Every handoff writes its results to `notes/<nn>-findings.md`. Code artifacts
   go in `apps/<name>/`. The notes directory is the shared memory between chats.
4. Handoff 09 is the capstone. Start it only when 01 and 05–08 have findings.

## Dependency graph

```
01 pty-recorder bake-off ──► 02 mini-mux ──► 03 web chat-view
        ▲                        ▲                ▲
        │                        │                │
   (APUE reading)          04 mux study      06 transcripts
                                             07 hooks

05 herdr socket API ──────────────────────────► 09 design record ◄── 08 protocols
01, 02, 03, 04, 06, 07 findings ──────────────►
inputs/*.md ──────────────────────────────────►
```

## Shared mental model (read once, assume everywhere)

**The PTY.** The kernel gives a terminal program a pseudo-terminal pair: a
master fd and a slave fd. The program writes UTF-8 text plus ANSI/VT escape
sequences to the slave; whoever holds the master reads that raw byte stream
and writes keystrokes back. No screens travel on the wire — the terminal
emulator holds a cell grid in memory and applies bytes to it. Window size
travels out-of-band (TIOCSWINSZ ioctl + SIGWINCH), not in the stream.

**A multiplexer is a headless terminal.** The server holds the PTY master for
every pane and runs an in-memory terminal emulator per pane. Clients are thin:
a socket connection streaming rendered output in, keystrokes out. Detach
closes the client; the server (the process's parent) keeps the PTY and the
child alive, and repaints from its grid on reattach.

**TUI output is paint commands, not a transcript.** Alternate screen, absolute
cursor addressing, partial redraws. You cannot recover "what the agent said"
from the byte stream without a full emulator — and then you get a screen, not
a conversation.

**Therefore: three sidecar channels carry the semantics.**
- *Semantic read*: the agent's own transcript files on disk (JSONL).
- *Control write*: input injection through whatever holds the PTY master
  (tmux send-keys, Herdr socket, your own master fd).
- *Events*: agent lifecycle hooks posting to a local socket.

Moshi's Chat View is built entirely on these three; it never parses the byte
stream. Herdr's integrations are mostly channel three plus session identity;
only its "screen manifest" fallback consumes the (already-emulated) grid.

**The design stance for Duo:** attach-to-terminal-session, not own-the-agent.
The session lives in the terminal; presentations (web, native, TUI) attach.
ACP-style protocols invert this — handoff 08 studies why, and where an ACP
backend could still slot in later.

## Conventions

- Findings notes: `notes/<nn>-findings.md`, headed with date + versions of
  every external tool touched (herdr, claude, codex, pi, opencode move fast).
- Verify external claims against live docs before relying on them; several
  handoffs exist precisely because docs and reality drift.
- Small artifacts over frameworks. Every build stage should stay readable in
  one sitting.

# Handoff 01 findings — PTY recorder bake-off (Bun/TS, Go, Rust)

Date: 2026-08-07

Tool versions: bun 1.3.13 · node v24.18.1 · go 1.26.5 · cargo 1.97.0 /
rustc 1.97.1 · claude v2.1.224 (Fable 5) · nvim 0.12.3 · python 3.12.13
(warm-up recorder) · Linux 6.8.0-136-generic.

All three implementations exist and pass the shared spec:
`apps/ptyrec-ts/`, `apps/ptyrec-go/`, `apps/ptyrec-rs/`. Each has a README
with run commands. Shared recordings live in `recordings/` (the
`claude-heavy-mid.raw` variant is the fidelity corpus — see "replay gotcha"
below).

## Headline findings

1. **node-pty is broken under Bun 1.3.13.** It installs and builds (after
   adding `node-gyp` as a direct devDependency), and small smoke tests pass.
   But under load it fails hard: relaying the firehose under `bun` died with
   SIGHUP (exit 129) in under 100 ms on 4/4 runs, capturing 19–195 KB of the
   88.9 MB stream at a random truncation point. Under `node` the identical
   code is 100 % reliable. Cause: node-pty's async write queue races Bun's
   process/pty teardown. Verdict: the TS track is really a **Node** track;
   Bun only runs the pure-JS replay side.
2. **All three headless emulators agree on the claude session.** The final
   grids from @xterm/headless, vt10x, and vt100 are byte-identical
   (vt100 differs only in a trailing newline). Parser fidelity at this
   corpus size does not differentiate the ecosystems.
3. **Parser throughput does differentiate.** Feeding the 88.9 MB firehose
   recording through each emulator: vt100 (Rust) 1.65 s, @xterm/headless
   2.61 s, vt10x (Go) 10.97 s. The expected "Rust and xterm ecosystems are
   deep, vt10x is thin" held up as a throughput gap (~4–6.6×), and as a
   completeness gap (vt10x lacks REP, below) — though vt10x was *not* thin
   on the claude corpus itself.
4. **Relay RSS separates the runtimes.** Rust 3.1 MB, Go 8.9 MB,
   Node 86.8 MB for the same job. Wall time is a wash (kernel-bound).

## Bench table

Relay: `ptyrec -o … -- seq 1 10000000` (88.9 MB after tty CRLF expansion).

| | Bun/TS (node) | Go | Rust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Firehose wall | 5.98 s | 5.64 s | 6.82 s |
| Firehose max RSS | 86.8 MB | 8.9 MB | 3.1 MB |
| Stalls / drops | none | none | none |
| Emulator | @xterm/headless | hinshun/vt10x | vt100 0.16.2 |
| Replay claude-heavy-mid (16 KB) | 70 ms (mostly startup) | 10 ms | ~2 ms |
| Replay RSS (16 KB corpus) | 51.6 MB | 3.8 MB | 2.6 MB |
| Emulator throughput (88.9 MB) | 2.61 s / 251 MB | 10.97 s / 184 MB | 1.65 s / 89 MB |
| LOC (src) | 224 | 355 | 313 |
| Deps | 28 pkgs, 104 MB node_modules (63 MB is node-pty) | 4 modules | 5 direct, 42 in lock |
| Clean build | `bun install` + native gyp build | 6.1 s | 13.0 s release |

Bun-runtime relay for comparison: **fails** (SIGHUP ≤100 ms, truncated
capture, 4/4 runs).

Note: the raw captures are byte-identical across languages except a 2-byte
trailing-drain difference in the Rust capture (88 888 899 vs 88 888 897).

## Stretch task — fidelity detail

Corpus: a real nested `claude` session (113 s, multi-Read turn, 16 272
bytes), truncated at byte 15 281 (t≈95 s, before exit cleanup) to
`claude-heavy-mid.raw`, replayed at 120×32.

- All three emulators reproduce the full Claude Code frame exactly: logo,
  prompt echo, tool-use line, the model's 3-bullet answer, separators,
  status line, `⏵⏵ auto mode` footer.
- **vt10x gap:** `CSI Ps b` (REP, repeat preceding character) is not
  implemented — `A\e[500b` yields one `A` plus blanks instead of 501 `A`s.
  Some TUIs use REP for run-length fills. No panics on truncated escapes or
  odd resize/scroll-region combos. Unexplored alternative if REP blocks:
  `charmbracelet/x/vt`.
- **wezterm-term is not on crates.io** (lives only in the wezterm git
  tree), so the Rust track used `vt100` (6-package dep tree). It handled
  truecolor SGR, DECSCUSR, and DA/DSR queries cleanly.
- **@xterm/headless** was flawless on every corpus; note its `write()` is
  async — read the buffer only from the completion callback.

**Replay-to-end gotcha (matters for the mux design):** a program that exits
cleanly emits alt-screen-exit / UI-cleanup sequences, so "apply the whole
file, dump the grid" shows the *post-exit* screen — often blank. The full
`claude-heavy.raw` replays to an empty grid; only the mid-turn truncation
shows content. This is correct emulation, and it is exactly why a mux
snapshots a *live* grid rather than replaying byte streams after the fact.

## Inspecting the raw streams

`claude-heavy.raw`: 16 272 bytes, 1 493 ESC sequences — 222 absolute cursor
addresses (CUP), 144 relative cursor moves, 377 SGR runs, 15 OSC, alt-screen
only for transient UI (claude renders mostly inline). 83 % of bytes are
printable, but they are *paint*, not prose: the same status line, spinner
("Zesting…", "Churned for 10s"), and token counter are redrawn dozens of
times, and the answer text appears interleaved with positioning. The vim
recording is starker: 22 598 bytes with 583 CUPs and one alt-screen
enter/exit pair wrapping everything.

Why this stream cannot be a conversation transcript: content and repaint are
indistinguishable without a full emulator; applying every byte yields a
*screen* (one 120×32 frame at one instant), not a dialogue; and the final
frame after clean exit is the cleaned-up shell, not the conversation at all.
Recovering "what the agent said" from this channel is a lossy screen-scrape
of whatever happened to be visible. The transcript has to come from the
agent's own JSONL sidecar — confirming the three-sidecar-channel
architecture in the README.

## Pain log (per language)

**Bun/TS** — `bun add node-pty` fails postinstall (`node-gyp: command not
found`) unless node-gyp is a direct devDependency; the Bun teardown race
above; @xterm/headless async write is easy to misuse; strict-mode
`argv[i]` indexing noise. node_modules is 104 MB for a 224-line tool.

**Go** — smoothest ride: zero build errors, first-compile API fit on all
three libs, defer-based termios restore just works. Footguns found were
harness-level, not language-level: EOF on ptyrec's stdin does not become
Ctrl-D on the slave, so piped test scripts must end in explicit `exit`; use
`bash --norc` for clean comparable recordings.

**Rust** — `portable-pty`'s `Box<dyn MasterPty>` is Send-not-Sync, so no
`Arc` sharing with the SIGWINCH thread; fix is to move the master into the
signal thread after `try_clone_reader()`/`take_writer()`. Must explicitly
`drop(pair.slave)` after spawn or the reader never sees EOF (doc-comment
knowledge, not type-level). `nix` needed a non-obvious `fs` feature for
`isatty`. A never-type coercion papercut in arg parsing. 13 s clean release
build vs Go's 6 s.

## Nix packaging outlook

- Go: `buildGoModule`, single static binary, trivial.
- Rust: `rustPlatform.buildRustPackage`, trivial (no pinned toolchain
  needed; plain nixpkgs rustc built it clean).
- Bun/TS: worst case — Bun's known autoPatchelfHook issue *plus* node-pty's
  node-gyp native build *plus* the runtime actually being Node. Packaging
  means shipping node_modules with a compiled `.node` artifact.

## Provisional recommendation for stage 02

**Engine in Go; keep the TS/xterm path warm for presentation. Rust is the
fallback if the emulator becomes the bottleneck.**

- The mux server (handoff 02) is mostly fd-plumbing, sessions, and a
  socket protocol — Go's sweet spot: fewest deps (4), fastest builds,
  no ownership friction around PTY handles, trivial Nix packaging, and
  8.9 MB RSS is fine for a resident daemon.
- Go's known weakness is exactly where the stretch task said it would be:
  vt10x is ~6.6× slower than vt100 and missing at least REP. For stage 02
  (repaint-on-reattach at human timescales, 16 KB-order sessions replaying
  in ~10 ms) that is nowhere near limiting. If profiling ever says
  otherwise, evaluate `charmbracelet/x/vt` before considering a rewrite.
- The hybrid split the handoff asked about looks right, but at a different
  seam than "engine Rust/Go, presentation TS": the *server* grid lives in
  Go, while the *web* presentation (handoff 03) should lean on
  @xterm/headless / xterm.js anyway — production-hardened, fast (2.61 s on
  88.9 MB), and native to the browser. Run it under Node, never Bun, and
  keep node-pty out of the picture (the server owns the PTYs; the web layer
  only consumes rendered state + sidecar channels).
- Rust won RSS and parser throughput and vt100 is excellent, but
  portable-pty's ownership/API friction and 2× build times buy nothing the
  mux needs yet. Revisit if the engine ever needs per-byte performance or
  wezterm-term's depth (vendored from the wezterm tree).

## Loose ends

- `recordings/` (claude-heavy, claude-heavy-mid, vim-smoke + timing files)
  is committed as the shared corpus for handoffs 02/06.
- Timing sidecars are valid NDJSON in all three implementations
  (`{"t": ms, "n": bytes}` per master read).
- Bench artifacts (per-run /usr/bin/time output, grids, diffs) were kept in
  the session scratchpad only; the table above is the durable record.

# Handoff 04 — Multiplexer architecture study (tmux, Zellij)

## Goal

Understand how production multiplexers structure server, client, protocol,
and grid — well enough to make mini-mux's design choices deliberately and to
recognize which parts Herdr re-derives. Reading and small experiments; no
build deliverable.

## Study list

1. **tmux server model.** `man tmux`: the client/server split, the socket in
   `/tmp/tmux-<uid>/`, `send-keys`, `capture-pane -p`, `pipe-pane -o`,
   `list-panes -F`. Then a source tour (github.com/tmux/tmux): where the PTY
   master is read, where the grid lives (`screen.c` / `grid.c`), how a client
   attach triggers a redraw. Depth: enough to narrate the path of one output
   byte from child to attached client.
2. **tmux control mode (`tmux -CC`).** The most instructive artifact in the
   whole study: a *textual client protocol* over the same socket, designed
   for programs (iTerm2 consumes it to render native panes). Run `tmux -CC`
   in a plain terminal, type commands, watch `%output`/`%layout-change`
   notifications. This is prior art for both mini-mux's protocol and any
   future Duo engine protocol.
3. **Zellij.** Architecture docs and source layout: Rust, server/client
   crates, its own `vt100`-style grid. Note what it added over tmux
   (layouts, plugin WASM runtime) and what that cost.
4. **Experiments** (30 min): drive a hidden tmux session entirely
   programmatically — `tmux new -d -s probe 'claude'`, `send-keys`,
   `capture-pane -p`, `pipe-pane` to a file — i.e. tmux as the "degenerate
   baseline backend" named in the feasibility record.

## Questions to answer in the notes

- What is the *minimum* verb set a mux client protocol needs? (Compare
  control mode's surface against mini-mux's plan in handoff 02.)
- How does tmux handle flow control / a slow client? Find the actual
  mechanism and describe it.
- Where does scrollback live, and what is the memory policy?
- What does tmux do on SIGWINCH when two differently-sized clients are
  attached? (The answer explains a classic mux annoyance.)
- Which of these problems does Herdr's socket API expose solutions for, and
  which does it hide?

## Deliverables

- `notes/04-findings.md`: the byte's-journey narrative, the protocol
  comparison table (control mode vs Zellij vs mini-mux plan vs Herdr), flow
  control answer, and 3–5 concrete design directives for handoff 02.

# tmux 3.4 internals — source-verified findings

Source: shallow clone of https://github.com/tmux/tmux at tag `3.4` (`git describe` → `3.4`), read at `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-dev-Code-terminal-multiplexers/54bc62d7-373e-4327-bcfb-1a5967240ca3/scratchpad/tmux`. All line numbers are from this tag, so they match the locally installed tmux 3.4 exactly.

## 1. The byte's journey (child process → attached client)

The server runs a single libevent loop: `server.c:252 proc_loop(server_proc, server_loop)` → `proc.c:213 proc_loop()`, which is literally `do event_loop(EVLOOP_ONCE); while (!tp->exit && !loopcb())` — one libevent pass, then `server.c:262 server_loop()` (which runs `server_client_loop()`), repeat.

**Step 1 — read the PTY master.** When a pane spawns, `window.c:1047 window_pane_set_event()` wraps the PTY master fd in a libevent bufferevent: `wp->event = bufferevent_new(wp->fd, window_pane_read_callback, NULL, window_pane_error_callback, wp)` (window.c:1051) and creates the parser context `wp->ictx = input_init(...)`. When the child writes, libevent fires **`window.c:1006 window_pane_read_callback()`**: it forwards new data to any `pipe-pane` fd, calls `control_write_output()` for every control-mode client, then calls `input_parse_pane(wp)` — and then `bufferevent_disable(wp->event, EV_READ)` (window.c:1030): reading is switched off after every read and only re-enabled by the flow-control check each loop (see §4).

Data is not consumed destructively: `input_parse_pane` (input.c:955) uses `window_pane_get_new_data(wp, &wp->offset, &new_size)` — per-consumer offsets (`struct window_pane_offset`) into the shared `wp->event->input` evbuffer, so the emulator, `pipe-pane`, and each control client each track their own read position (window.c:1560–1600).

**Step 2 — parse.** `input.c:967 input_parse_buffer()` starts a screen-write context (`screen_write_start_pane(sctx, wp, &wp->base)` — pane's base screen; NULL pane if a mode like copy-mode is active so the tty is not updated), then `input.c:896 input_parse()` runs the byte through a table-driven VT state machine (`struct input_state`/`input_transition`; ground state table at input.c:483: bytes 0x20–0x7e → `input_print`). A printable byte lands in `input.c:1137 input_print()` → `screen_write_collect_add(sctx, &ictx->cell.cell)` (the "collect" fast path batches consecutive printed characters; any non-print handler first calls `screen_write_collect_end` — input.c:933).

**Step 3 — mutate the grid.** `screen-write.c:1936 screen_write_cell()` (called directly for wide/UTF-8 cells, and by `screen_write_collect_end` for batched runs) writes into the pane's grid via `grid_view_set_cell` → `grid.c:549 grid_set_cell()`. Data structures (tmux.h:716–777):
- `struct grid` — `sx, sy`, plus `hscrolled`, `hsize`, `hlimit` and a single `linedata` array of `hsize + sy` lines (history and visible screen are one array; "view" coordinates are offset by `hsize` — `grid-view.c`).
- `struct grid_line` — `celldata` (array of `grid_cell_entry`), `cellused/cellsize`, `extddata` (array of `grid_extd_entry`), `flags` (`GRID_LINE_WRAPPED`, `GRID_LINE_EXTENDED`…), `time`.
- `struct grid_cell_entry` (packed, 5 bytes) — union of `{attr, fg, bg, data}` single bytes, or an `offset` into the line's `extddata` when `GRID_FLAG_EXTENDED` is set. This is the extended-cell mechanism: cells that need UTF-8 >1 byte, 256/RGB colour, underscore colour, or hyperlinks get a `struct grid_extd_entry` (utf8_char + full attrs, grid.c:114 `grid_extended_cell`, grid.c:100 `grid_get_extended_cell`); plain ASCII+8-colour cells stay 5 bytes (`grid.c:61 grid_store_cell`).
- `screen_write_cell` also has a `skip` optimization (screen-write.c:2004–2027): if the new cell equals the stored cell byte-for-byte, it neither writes the grid nor emits to ttys.

**Step 4 — fan out to clients.** tmux does **not** forward raw bytes. Each screen-write operation builds a `struct tty_ctx` (`screen-write.c:172 screen_write_initctx`) and calls **`tty.c:1713 tty_write(cmdfn, ctx)`**, which loops `TAILQ_FOREACH(c, &clients, entry)` and calls the command function once per ready client: e.g. `tty_write(tty_cmd_cell, &ttyctx)` (screen-write.c:2067), `tty_cmd_cells` for collected runs (screen-write.c:1810). `tty.c:2129 tty_cmd_cell()` clips against that client's visible region/overlays, then re-emits fresh escape sequences generated from that client's terminfo (`tty_attributes`, `tty_cell`, `tty_putc`) — per-client re-emission, sizes and capabilities can differ per client. Bytes end up in `tty_add()` (tty.c:585): `evbuffer_add(tty->out, ...)` + `event_add(&tty->event_out)`; libevent's `tty.c:239 tty_write_callback()` flushes `tty->out` to the client's real tty fd with `evbuffer_write`.

So the journey: child write(2) → PTY master → libevent → `window_pane_read_callback` → `input_parse` state machine → `screen_write_*` → `grid_set_cell` (authoritative state) **and, in the same pass,** `tty_write` → per-client `tty_cmd_*` → per-client escape-sequence synthesis → `tty->out` evbuffer → `tty_write_callback` → client terminal.

## 2. Input path (keystroke → PTY)

The client passes its real tty fd to the server over the socket (imsg fd passing: `server-client.c:2926 server_client_dispatch_identify`, `MSG_IDENTIFY_TTYNAME` at :2981, fd via `imsg_get_fd`; `tty_init` at server-client.c:3045). The **server** then reads keys directly from that fd: `tty.c:164 tty_read_callback` → `tty_keys_next()` (tty-keys.c:660) parses escape sequences into `key_code`s → `server_client_handle_key()` (server-client.c:2059) queues `server_client_key_callback` (server-client.c:1851) on the command queue → key-binding lookup, else `window_pane_key()` (window.c:1179) → `input_key_pane()` (input-keys.c:406) → `input_key()` translates the key back into bytes appropriate for the pane's modes and writes them with `input_key_write(__func__, wp->event, buf, len)` (input-keys.c:685 and friends) — i.e. `bufferevent_write` on the PTY master.

## 3. Attach / redraw

`cmd-attach-session.c` (~line 128/152) calls `server_client_set_session(c, s)`; that function (server-client.c) ends with `recalculate_sizes()` … `server_redraw_client(c)`. `server-fn.c:33 server_redraw_client()` just sets `c->flags |= CLIENT_ALLREDRAWFLAGS`. On the next `server_client_loop()` pass, `server_client_check_redraw()` (server-client.c:2572–2662) sees the flags and calls **`screen-redraw.c:567 screen_redraw_screen(c)`** → `screen_redraw_draw_panes()` (screen-redraw.c:769) → `screen_redraw_draw_pane()` which loops the pane's rows calling **`tty.c:1424 tty_draw_line(tty, s, …)`** — reading cells straight out of `wp->screen`'s grid and synthesizing escape output. Confirmed: repaint is a pure function of the in-memory grid; the PTY byte history is never replayed (it isn't even kept — the evbuffer is drained, §4).

## 4. Flow control / slow clients

Three distinct mechanisms:

**(a) PTY read gating (pane side).** `window_pane_read_callback` disables `EV_READ` after every read (window.c:1030). Each server loop, `server-client.c:2246 server_client_check_pane_buffer()` computes the minimum consumed offset across all consumers (emulator `wp->offset`, `pipe-pane` offset, and every control client's `control_pane_offset`), drains that many bytes: `evbuffer_drain(evb, minimum)` (server-client.c:2298), and maintains `wp->base_offset` with explicit `SIZE_MAX` wrap handling. Then the `off` decision (server-client.c:2326–2331): if all attached clients are control clients that cannot accept more data, `bufferevent_disable(wp->event, EV_READ)` — tmux stops reading the PTY and the child eventually blocks in write(2); otherwise `bufferevent_enable(EV_READ)`. Note: an ordinary (non-control) attached client always forces reading on (`off = 0`) — normal clients never stall the pane; there is no `READ_SIZE` constant in 3.4 (that was the older mechanism; 3.4 uses this offset scheme).

**(b) Normal client backpressure = discard, not block.** `tty.c:85–87`: `TTY_BLOCK_INTERVAL` (100 ms), `TTY_BLOCK_START(tty)` = `1 + sx*sy*8` bytes, `TTY_BLOCK_STOP(tty)` = `1 + sx*sy/8`. `tty.c:210 tty_block_maybe()`: if `EVBUFFER_LENGTH(tty->out)` exceeds BLOCK_START, set `TTY_BLOCK`, drain the whole buffer, and start a 100 ms timer. While blocked, `tty_add()` (tty.c:585) throws output away, counting `tty->discarded`. The timer callback (`tty_timer_callback`, tty.c:193) unblocks once a 100 ms interval discards less than BLOCK_STOP, then sets `c->flags |= CLIENT_ALLREDRAWFLAGS` (tty.c:197) — a slow client silently loses intermediate frames and gets a full grid repaint when it catches up. Classic "headless terminal" behavior.

**(c) Control-mode flow control (control.c).** Control clients are exact-byte consumers, so discarding is not allowed; instead: each pane has a per-client offset queue (big comment control.c:24–45, `struct control_pane`/`control_block`). `control.c:433 control_check_age()`: if the oldest unsent block is older than the client's `pause_age` and the client set `CLIENT_CONTROL_PAUSEAFTER` (via `refresh-client -f pause-after=N` — parsed in server-client.c:3104–3108), the pane is paused: `control_write(c, "%%pause %%%u")` (`control_pause_pane`, control.c:375); the client resumes it with `refresh-client -A '%<pane>:continue'` → `control_continue_pane` → `%continue` (control.c:369; cmd-refresh-client.c:153–157 maps `-A` on/off/continue). Without pause mode, a client more than `CONTROL_MAXIMUM_AGE` (300000 ms, control.c:138) behind is killed with exit message "too far behind" (control.c:457–459). Other flags: `no-output` (`CLIENT_CONTROL_NOOUTPUT`), `wait-exit` (`CLIENT_CONTROL_WAITEXIT`) — tmux.h:1851–1858. Paused/`off` control panes are what can flip `off=1` in mechanism (a).

## 5. Scrollback

History and screen are one allocation: `grid->linedata` holds `hsize + sy` lines; `hsize`/`hscrolled`/`hlimit` in `struct grid` (tmux.h:765–777). A linefeed at the bottom of a `GRID_HISTORY` grid goes `grid-view.c:85` → `grid_collect_history()` then `grid_scroll_history()` (grid.c:354, 396): scroll = `xreallocarray` one more line, `hsize++` — the top screen line simply *becomes* history, no copying. Enforcement: `grid_collect_history` (grid.c:354) runs on every scroll; once `hsize >= hlimit` it frees the oldest 10% of `hlimit` (min 1 line) via `grid_trim_history` (grid.c:342, `grid_free_lines` + `memmove`) — so history briefly oscillates around the limit rather than being trimmed line-by-line. Allocation is per-pane: `spawn.c:246` reads session option `history-limit` (default 2000, `options-table.c:540`; range 0–INT_MAX) at pane creation → `window_add_pane(w, …, hlimit, …)` → `screen_init(&wp->base, sx, sy, hlimit)` (window.c:948); changing the option does not affect existing panes. Lines are plain `grid_line` cell arrays — no compression — but on entering history a line is compacted: `grid_compact_line` (grid.c:142, called at grid.c:406) rebuilds `extddata` to drop unreferenced extended entries; also `grid_empty_line`s allocate `celldata` lazily.

## 6. Two clients of different sizes / SIGWINCH

Option `window-size` (options-table.c:1166): choices largest/smallest/manual/latest (constants tmux.h:1219–1222), **default `WINDOW_SIZE_LATEST`** in 3.4 (`.default_num = WINDOW_SIZE_LATEST`). Computation: `resize.c:114 clients_calculate_size()` iterates attached clients; for LARGEST it takes max sx/sy, for SMALLEST min, for LATEST it only considers `w->latest` (the client that most recently sent input; updated in `server_client_update_latest`) when more than one client is on the window (resize.c:167). Entry points: `resize.c:285 default_window_size()` (new windows) and `resize.c:360 recalculate_size()` per window, called from `resize.c:427 recalculate_sizes()` (invoked on attach, detach, and client SIGWINCH — the client relays its winsize via `MSG_RESIZE`, and the server clamps to `TTY_SX/sy` limits). A window smaller than a given client's terminal: `screen_redraw_screen` classifies cells outside the window as `CELL_OUTSIDE` (screen-redraw.c:233/293) and `screen_redraw_border_set` (screen-redraw.c:50) draws them — by default `CELL_BORDERS[CELL_OUTSIDE]` = `'~'` **with `GRID_ATTR_CHARSET`** (screen-redraw.c:62–64; `CELL_BORDERS " xqlkmjwvtun~"`, tmux.h:711), i.e. the ACS glyph for `~` = the bullet `·` — those are the famous dots. The `fill-character` window option (options-table.c:943, applied at screen-redraw.c:55 via `w->fill_character`, set in `window_set_fill_character`, window.c:1641) overrides them.

## 7. Control mode (`tmux -CC`)

Confirmed: a control client is an ordinary `struct client` on the same UNIX socket with `CLIENT_CONTROL` set; instead of a tty, `control.c:770ff control_start()` attaches bufferevents (`read_event`/`write_event`) with `control_read_callback` / `control_write_callback` doing a line-based text protocol over the client's stdin/stdout fds. Commands in: `control_read_callback` (control.c:546) does `evbuffer_readln(…EVBUFFER_EOL_LF)` per line and feeds `cmd_parse_and_append`; an empty line detaches. Responses out: every command executed for a control client is framed by `cmdq_guard` (cmd-queue.c:816): `%begin <time> <number> <flags>` before (cmd-queue.c:619, control.c:527), then output, then `%end` or `%error` with the same time/number (cmd-queue.c:668–670) — that triple lets the client match replies to requests. Pane output: `window_pane_read_callback` calls `control_write_output(c, wp)` (control.c:468) per control client; `control_append_data` (control.c:609) builds `%output %<pane> <data>` (or `%extended-output %<pane> <age> : <data>` when `CLIENT_CONTROL_PAUSEAFTER`), escaping every byte `< 0x20` and `\` as `\%03o` octal (control.c:632–635). Asynchronous notifications come from `control-notify.c`: `%layout-change`, `%window-add`/`%unlinked-window-add`, `%window-close`, `%window-renamed`, `%window-pane-changed`, `%pane-mode-changed`, `%session-changed`, `%client-session-changed`, `%client-detached`, `%session-renamed`, `%sessions-changed`, `%session-window-changed`, `%paste-buffer-changed`, `%paste-buffer-deleted`, plus `%pause`/`%continue` from control.c (see §4c). Ordering discipline: `%output` is deferred into per-pane blocks so command replies and output interleave in a consistent order (comment control.c:24–45).

Socket path: `tmux.c:187 make_label()` — `xasprintf(&base, "%s/tmux-%ld", path, (long)uid)` (tmux.c:209) where `path` is `TMUX_SOCK`/`/tmp`; default label "default" → `/tmp/tmux-<uid>/default`; `-L` changes the label, `-S` overrides the path entirely (tmux.c:494ff). First client startup: `client.c` tries to connect; on failure it calls `server.c:175 server_start()`, which `proc_fork_and_daemon(&fd)` (server.c:188) — fork + daemonize, keeping a socketpair to the founding client — then `event_reinit`, creates the listening socket (`server_create_socket`, server.c:106, `bind`+`listen`, mode influenced by `server_update_socket` at server.c:331: socket loses +x when no session is attached), makes the founding client with `server_client_create(fd)`, and enters `proc_loop(server_proc, server_loop)`. One server process per socket path; it holds the global `RB_TREE`s of `sessions`, `windows`, `all_window_panes` (initialized server.c:210–214) — many sessions, many clients, one event loop.
